texts: Describe the structure and function of the parts of the human eye (e.g. cornea, lens, sclera, choroid, retina, rods & cones, fovea centralis, pupil, iris and optic nerve)
Describe the structure and function of the parts of the human ear (e.g. pinna, auditory canal, tympanum, ossicles, cochlea, organ of Corti, auditory nerve, semicircular canals and Eustachian tube)
Explain other ways that humans sense their environment and their spatial orientation within it (i.e. olfactory receptors, taste receptors, touch receptors)

When a ray of sunlight hits your skin, sensory receptors send a message to the brain, which receives and processes this information, causing you to feel warmth.

Another example is when you walk into a coffee shop and smell the fresh smell of coffee, but after a while you are not aware of it. Or when you no longer hear/notice a background noise.

There are many different types of receptors in the skin that respond to a variety of different stimuli such as touch, pressure, temperature, pain, and various intensities of these. (You do not need to have any of this memorized, just appreciate the complexity! )

is a location in the retina that contains a high concentration of cones, while the
(the point at which the optic nerve connects to the retina) contains neither rods nor cones. This is why when light falls on the blind spot, no image is generated.

eyeball is slightly elongated, so focused light falls in front of the retina
nearsighted people can wear concave lenses to help focus light directly on the retina

eyeball is slightly shortened, so focused light falls behind the retina
farsighted people can wear convex lenses to help focus light directly on the retina
The retina is composed of two types of light-sensitive photoreceptors:
Rods respond to low-intensity light to detect black and white.
We rely on rods during low light or nighttime vision
Cones respond to high-intensity light to identify colour.
We rely on cones to general high visual detail when there is an abundance of light
The lens generates an inverted image on the retina, but the brain flips the received message to generate an upright perceived image.
is a genetic condition caused by a lack of specific cones, or colour receptors.
Most color blind individuals lack the cones which respond to red-green wavelengths, so they cannot perceive those colours (see them as shades of brown)
Rods contain a light-sensitive pigment called
, a form of vitamin A. Thus, a lack of vitamin A can lead to what is commonly referred to as “night blindness”.
In humans, development of the eye and brain structures is only partially complete upon birth.
Newborns are thought to see the world “upside down” for the first few days until their brain learns to properly interpret the info it is receiving
Hearing is associated with small fluctuations in air pressure, called
. Mechanoreceptors in the inner ear convert the energy of sound waves into electrochemical impulses which the brain perceives as sound...
generating vibrations within the middle ear.
When sound waves push against the tympanum, its vibrations are
a set of three small connected bones, called the
, causing changes in pressure within the organs of the inner ear
Changes in pressure stimulate the movement of hair cells (collectively known as the
, generating an action potential within the
This action potential is carried to the temporal lobes by the auditory nerve, where sound information is processed and interpreted.
Parts of the Ear not Involved with Hearing

: Three fluid filled canals in each of the three dimensions with hair cells that respond to movement → provides information about
Extra: Utricle and Saccule: Provide information about body position and acceleration
Balance disorders commonly result from damage to the semicircular canals, including...
leakage of inner ear fluid after head injury or dramatic changes in air pressure, causing dizziness and nausea
failure of canals to flex properly in response to a change in head position, causing dizziness (vertigo)
an increase in fluid volume, leading to a ringing or buzzing and a feeling of fullness in the ear
Parts of the Ear not Involved with Hearing
is an opening that connects the middle ear with the nasal cavity, and acts to equalize pressure in the middle ear. This is what is commonly fels as your ears popping
Hearing loss may be caused by a number of factors, including:
Improper development of any of the organs required for
hearing can lead to deafness; often hereditary, but can sometimes be treated with cochlear implants
Swelling of the middle ear can prevent sound waves from
reaching the cochlea; in some cases, structures of the middle ear can become permanently damaged
Loud noises can damage hair cells within the cochlea or
even cause the tympanic membrane to rupture
